There's a plastic wall inside your phone thinner than most human hairs. If it fails, your phone can catch fire. 🔥

It keeps your battery's two sides apart, so electrons have to take the long way round, through your phone. Pierce it, and they take the shortcut. That's what happened inside some Galaxy Note 7 batteries in 2016.

In 11 days, one hacking group hit 200+ organisations in 14 countries, and AI did most of the work.
Security firm CrowdStrike says a China-linked group it calls Vapor Panda ran a team of AI agents, mostly on the Chinese model DeepSeek. One human gave the orders; the agents tried several ways in at once and switched when one failed. Targets included foreign ministries, defence and chip firms, and phone networks, with confirmed break-ins at nine. The eye-opener is speed: a human runs maybe 40 commands an hour, these agents could top 1,500. A year ago, the first known AI-run spy campaign hit about 30 targets. Now it's 200+. The boring basics still matter most: updates and two-step logins.

18102122606533473.media_caption:
In August 2010, one bitcoin payment created 184 billion bitcoin out of nothing. Only 21 million should ever exist.
Early developer Jeff Garzik spotted block 74,638 paying two wallets 92 billion BTC each and posted "Strange block". The code added the two amounts without checking their size, so the total rolled over like a mileage counter and looked tiny. That night Satoshi Nakamoto posted a fix; by morning the fixed chain had taken over and the coins were gone.
The 21 million limit holds because every computer running Bitcoin checks the same code. Wrong code, wrong limit.

Your crypto wallet doesn't hold any crypto. It holds 12 or 24 recovery words, and whoever sees them can take everything.
In April 2025, scammers mailed letters posing as Ledger: a QR code and a threat to enter your recovery words or lose access. In February 2026, Trezor owners got one with a deadline.
The trick needs two mistakes: trusting a deadline, and typing your words into a website. There's no undo. Enter them only on your own wallet. Ledger and Trezor never ask.

18141991825714771.media_caption:
If Bitcoin fell to $1, the miners keeping it running would earn about $3 a block. A thought experiment, not a prediction.
Today each block pays about 3.13 bitcoin, roughly $240,000. At $1 that's $3, far below the power bill (mining uses about 0.5% of the world's electricity), so most machines would switch off. Fewer machines means slower blocks: when China banned mining in 2021, a third of mining power went dark and one block took 129 minutes. Then Bitcoin's built-in reset made the puzzle 28% easier, the biggest cut ever. The network survives. Holders don't: Strategy paid about $64 billion for 848,517 bitcoin that would be worth under $1 million. The rules protect the network, not the price. Critics say that's the risk.
